newsitem.title: USA: Business group unveils Social Security reform plan.
newsitem.headline: Business group unveils Social Security reform plan.

text.p: Wading into the debate over the future of Social Security, a business group Thursday proposed radical changes to the system aimed at averting a Social Security funding crisis.

The Committee for Economic Development's reform plan would scale back benefits and require individuals to set up personal retirement accounts. Under the plan 3 percent of paychecks would be contributed to savings accounts, which would operate much like current tax-deferred individual retirement accounts.

The mandatory contribution would be in addition to current Social Security payroll taxes. Employees and employers would split the amount equally while self-employed workers would pay the full levy of 3 percent.

Bruce MacLaury, chairman of the project, said the changes would protect the solvency of Social Security, which is projected to go broke by 2029, while increasing the rate of return to many individuals and improving overall U.S. savings.

The Committee for Economic Development represents 250 business executives and academics across the nation. Social Security faces a funding crisis in coming years as baby boomers retire and a smaller pool of workers struggles to fund the system.
The committee's plan is one of a spate of recent proposals for shoring up Social Security, most of which call for investment in private markets to increase the program's rate of return.

The latest plan would gradually raise the Social Security retirement age to 70 from 65 by 2030, reduce average benefits for middle- and upper-income recipients, increase the number of years a person must work to get full benefits and increase the amount of Social Security checks subject to taxation.
The personal retirement accounts required under the plan would be owned and managed by individuals, who could invest in a limited number of private-sector financial securities.
MacLaury denied the mandatory contribution was a tax.

"None of these funds goes to a government entity. None of it may be spent by a government entity," said MacLaury, president emeritus of the Brookings Institution. "It's hard to see that money that never touches the hands of a civil servant" could be a tax.

A divided presidential commission last month issued a long-awaited report laying out three conflicting strategies for protecting Social Security. The options ranged from investing part of the Social Security trust fund in private markets to broad plans for individual investment accounts.
Congress has held hearings on the issue, but lawmakers are in no hurry to make major changes to the popular progam.
Under the Committee for Economic Development's plan account earnings would accumulate on a tax-deferred basis. The plan does not allow for early withdrawals or borrowing from funds before retirement.

MacLaury said companies that now have pension plans could redirect part of current pension contributions to the personal retirement accounts to meet the 1.5 percent investment requirement. He admitted upper-income individuals might not fare as well under the new plan, but would be better off than if Congress increased taxes to shore up the system.
